name: The Hundred
shortDescription: A breath-driven warm-up that engages the abdominals while pumping the arms and stabilizing the ribcage.
benefits: Improves lung capacity and steady core support through intentional breath pacing.
modifications: Keep the head on the mat and legs lower to reduce cervical strain and core load.
Perform single-leg pumps or supported heel taps if full leg extension is too intense.
If the client has vision or hearing impairment, keep the space clutter-free, use clear tactile and visual cues, and avoid fast verbal timing.
For immunosuppression, recent recovery, or sensitive skin, choose clean props, gentle regressions, and avoid direct pressure on irritated areas.
progressions: Extend the legs higher while keeping the pelvis stable.
Increase arm speed slightly once breath coordination is steady.
breathing: Inhale for five pumps, exhale for five pumps; keep the ribs long and shoulders relaxed.
setup: Lie supine with knees bent in tabletop, shoulders relaxed, and arms long by your sides.
instructions: Lie supine with knees bent in tabletop, shoulders relaxed, and arms long by your sides.
Lift your head, neck and shoulders off the mat while keeping the lower back grounded.
Pump your arms vigorously in small motions alongside the body.
Coordinate the movement with breath: inhale for five pumps, exhale for five pumps.
Stay steady through the ribs and avoid pressing the shoulders into the ears.
Regression: Keep the head on the mat and legs lower to reduce cervical strain and core load.
Progression: Extend the legs higher while keeping the pelvis stable.
commonMistakes: Allowing the lower back to arch away from the mat.
Tensing the shoulders or lifting them toward the ears.
keyTakeaway: Focus on core endurance and breathing coordination
safetyNote: Maintain even breathing, keep the spine supported, and stop if any sharp pain or breath-holding occurs.
whereToFeel: Feel the work in the abdominals and inner thighs as you stabilize the ribcage.
transitionIn: Lie supine with knees bent in tabletop, arms by your sides, and prepare for breath.
transitionOut: Lower the head and feet to the mat, then roll to your side to sit up safely.
contraindicationsNote: If the client has osteoporosis, pregnancy, recent injury, vision or hearing impairment, immunosuppression, sensitive skin, ankylosing spondylitis or other spinal conditions, shoulder or elbow issues, foot/ankle or knee problems, chronic pain, or other medical conditions, consult a qualified instructor or clinician.

name: Roll Up
shortDescription: Sequential spinal articulation from supine to seated that builds core strength while lengthening the back.
benefits: Builds deep abdominal control while teaching safe spinal articulation.
modifications: Bend the knees and use the arms to support the spine during the roll-up.
Start with a tabletop prep variation if hamstring flexibility is limited.
If the client has vision or hearing impairment, keep the space clutter-free, use clear tactile and visual cues, and avoid fast verbal timing.
For immunosuppression, recent recovery, or sensitive skin, choose clean props, gentle regressions, and avoid direct pressure on irritated areas.
progressions: Perform with straight legs and less use of the arms.
Lift the arms overhead to increase the challenge once the spine is stable.
breathing: Exhale to peel the spine up, inhale at the top, then exhale to articulate down.
setup: Lie supine with legs straight and arms reaching overhead, pelvis neutral, and ribs soft.
instructions: Lie supine with legs straight, arms reaching overhead, and the pelvis neutral.
Inhale to lengthen through the spine and keep the shoulders wide and relaxed.
Exhale to peel the spine up one vertebra at a time, reaching forward from the hips.
Hold the top with the abdominals engaged and the lower ribs drawn in.
Inhale to initiate the descent, then exhale to articulate the spine down slowly.
Regression: Bend the knees and use the arms to support the spine during the roll-up.
Progression: Perform with straight legs and less use of the arms.
commonMistakes: Using momentum instead of articulating the spine.
Pulling on the neck as you rise.
keyTakeaway: Focus on spinal articulation and abdominal mobility
safetyNote: Keep the neck long, avoid pulling on the head, and stop if the lower back lifts away from the mat.
whereToFeel: Primary sensation: abdominals and spinal flexors during the roll and hamstrings in the stretch.
transitionIn: Lie supine with legs straight and arms overhead, pelvis neutral.
transitionOut: After the last rep, bend the knees and roll to your side before sitting up.
contraindicationsNote: If the client has osteoporosis, pregnancy, recent injury, vision or hearing impairment, immunosuppression, sensitive skin, ankylosing spondylitis or other spinal conditions, shoulder or elbow issues, foot/ankle or knee problems, chronic pain, or other medical conditions, consult a qualified instructor or clinician.

name: Roll Over
shortDescription: Controlled inversion and spine mobility exercise that opens the back line and stretches the hamstrings.
benefits: Enhances back flexibility and helps stretch the posterior chain.
modifications: Keep the legs bent and move with a smaller range of motion to protect the hamstrings and lower back.
Use the arms to support the motion and roll only as far as the shoulders allow.
If the client has vision or hearing impairment, keep the space clutter-free, use clear tactile and visual cues, and avoid fast verbal timing.
For immunosuppression, recent recovery, or sensitive skin, choose clean props, gentle regressions, and avoid direct pressure on irritated areas.

Lower the legs more slowly toward vertical while keeping the spine controlled.
breathing: Exhale to lift the legs overhead, inhale at the top, then exhale to lower with control.

instructions: Lie supine with legs straight and arms alongside the body.
Inhale to prepare, draw the abdominals in, and keep the ribs soft.
Exhale to lift the legs overhead and roll onto the shoulders with control.
Pause at the top with the pelvis stable and the legs long.
Inhale at the top, then exhale to lower the legs back down slowly while keeping the lower back supported.

commonMistakes: Dropping the legs too quickly and losing core control.
Collapsing the lower back during the roll.

safetyNote: Move slowly, keep the lower back anchored, and choose a regression if the hamstrings or neck feel strained.
whereToFeel: Feel the stretch in the hamstrings and the control in the lower abdominals.
transitionIn: Lie supine with legs straight, arms by your sides, and lower back anchored.
transitionOut: Lower the legs, roll to your side, and use your hands to help you sit up.
